notes.meaning: Early in the morning, the chief priests and elders gathered to make formal plans to put Jesus to death. They met at sunrise to make their plot appear lawful, since Jewish law did not permit capital trials to be held at night. They had already decided He was guilty, and now they planned how to persuade the Roman governor to execute Him.

The religious leaders tied Jesus' hands and marched Him through the streets of Jerusalem to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Under Roman rule, the Jewish council did not have the authority to carry out an execution, so they needed the civil ruler to do it. Jesus willingly accepted these bonds so that sinners could be set free from the chains of guilt.

When Judas saw that Jesus was condemned to die, he was struck with deep remorse and brought the thirty silver coins back to the rulers. He may have expected Jesus to escape by a miracle, and the realization of what he had done crushed him with guilt. His sorrow was not a true repentance that turned to God for pardon, but the misery of an awakened conscience trapped in despair.

Judas openly admitted his sin and insisted that Jesus was completely innocent. The chief priests coldly brushed him off, telling him that his guilt was his own problem and none of their concern. Their cruel answer shows that partners in evil offer no real comfort when the horror of sin sets in.

Judas threw the silver coins into the temple sanctuary and ran off to hang himself. The money he had coveted brought him only agony, and throwing it away could not quiet his guilty conscience. Because he abandoned all hope in God's mercy, his despair ended in self-destruction.

The chief priests picked up the coins but refused to put them into the sacred temple treasury because they were the price paid for a man's life. They scrupulously kept religious rules about gifts while actively working to murder an innocent man. Their behavior shows how hypocrites can be very careful about small traditions while ignoring God's law of justice.

After talking it over, the priests used the silver to buy a potter's field as a cemetery for foreign visitors who died in Jerusalem. The land was cheap because its clay was exhausted and it was useless for farming. Many teachers see this purchase as a picture of how the blood of Jesus provides a resting place of mercy even for outsiders and Gentiles.

The plot of land became widely known among the people as the Field of Blood because it was bought with money paid to betray Jesus. The priests hoped to cover their crime by doing an act of public charity, but the name preserved the memory of their guilt. God often makes sure that wicked deeds are not easily hidden or forgotten.

Matthew explains that these events fulfilled the ancient prophecy about thirty silver coins being used to purchase a potter's field. Thirty pieces of silver was the legal price of an ordinary slave, showing how little the rulers of Israel valued the Son of God. Even in the middle of human wickedness, God's sovereign plan was moving forward exactly as He had ordained.

differ.view: The name Jeremiah likely entered the text through a scribe's copy error, while Matthew was paraphrasing the meaning of Zechariah's prophecy.
Jeremiah may have spoken the prophecy first before Zechariah recorded it, or Jeremiah's name stood for the entire prophetic scroll because his book was placed first.
Matthew quoted freely from memory, blending themes from both Jeremiah and Zechariah together.

notes.meaning: Jesus stood as a prisoner before Pontius Pilate, who asked Him if He claimed to be the King of the Jews. Jesus acknowledged the title, though His kingdom was spiritual and posed no political threat to the Roman Empire. The Son of God willingly stood on trial before an earthly judge so that believers could stand pardoned before God.

When the chief priests and elders shouted repeated accusations against Him, Jesus remained completely silent. Their slanders carried their own confutation and were unworthy of an answer. He held His peace because He had willingly submitted to His Father's plan to offer Himself as a sacrifice for sin.

Pilate pressed Jesus to speak and defend Himself against the long list of charges brought by the rulers. The governor felt no personal hatred toward Jesus and wanted Him to clear Himself of the accusations. He was surprised that a man facing the death penalty would make no effort to save His own life.

Jesus refused to answer a single word, leaving the Roman governor deeply astonished at His quiet composure. Roman rulers were used to hearing prisoners beg desperately for mercy, but Jesus displayed calm dignity and refused to trade insults. His patient silence fulfilled the prophecy that the suffering servant would be led like a lamb to the slaughter without opening His mouth.

Each year during the Passover feast, the Roman governor had a custom of setting free any one prisoner chosen by the crowd. This practice was adopted by the Romans to please the Jewish people and reduce unrest during the crowded festival. Pilate hoped this tradition would provide a way to release Jesus without confronting the priests directly.

At that time, the Romans held an infamous prisoner named Barabbas. He was widely known as a dangerous outlaw who had taken part in a violent rebellion and committed murder. Pilate considered him such an obvious menace that he assumed the people would never want him back on the streets.

Pilate asked the assembled crowd whether they wanted him to release Barabbas or Jesus who was called the Christ. He expected the people to reject a violent criminal and choose the peaceful teacher. By using the title of Christ, Pilate reminded them of Jesus' widespread standing as the promised Messiah.

Pilate knew full well that the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of pure envy. The leaders were jealous because the people admired Jesus' teaching and miracles, which exposed their own lack of spiritual authority. An honest judge would have dismissed charges based on malice, but Pilate lacked the moral courage to do what was right.

While sitting on the judgment seat, Pilate received an urgent message from his wife telling him not to condemn this innocent man. God had given her a terrifying dream that warned her that harming Jesus would bring down divine judgment. Even when Jesus' disciples were silent, God used a Roman woman to declare the innocence of His Son.

The chief priests and elders went through the crowd and persuaded them to demand Barabbas and call for Jesus to be destroyed. The leaders used their authority and influence to stir up mob anger against a man who had done only good among them. This tragic scene shows how easily people can be led into terrible evil when they blindly follow corrupt guides.

When the governor asked the people once more to make their choice, the crowd shouted for Barabbas. Swayed by their leaders, they chose a murderer over the holy Son of God. People still make this tragic trade whenever they choose the world and sin instead of Christ.

Pilate asked the crowd what he should do with Jesus, and they all demanded that He be crucified. Crucifixion was the most shameful, painful death known, reserved for rebels and the lowest criminals. The very crowd that had recently hailed Jesus with praises now demanded His death, showing how quickly human favor can vanish.
